newsitem.title: UK: Physical tin slumbers as 4th quarter 1996 beckons.
newsitem.headline: Physical tin slumbers as 4th quarter 1996 beckons.

text.p: Physical tin business in Europe is running at a low ebb at present, as the end of the summer shutdowns and approach of the final quarter of the year has brought little discernible pick-up in activity.
Since the end of July, London Metal Exchange (LME) tin prices have been trapped between around $6,100 and $6,300 a tonne, with action recently restricted to the mid-$6,200 area.
"The Chinese are looking to sell at the higher end...and there is consumer interest at the lower end. So it is steady, but very quiet," one trader said.
"This is very much a market that is moving sideways. Consumers have come in (to the market), but not to any great extent," another trader said.
Much of the business taking place reflects transactions booked on long-term contracts, with spot requirements remaining thin on the ground, he said.

Premiums in Europe have hardly moved over the last month as well, and other traders said that producers and consumers are looking to trade more with each other, and not rely so much on the merchant fraternity.
"The producers appear to be marketing directly to the consumers, looking to keep the trade out of it," one said.

Meanwhile, warehouse stock movements are looking favourable for longer-term price movement. LME inventories have fallen from mid-August levels of 10,795 tonnes to a current 10,115 tonnes, largely due to a 525-tonne drawdown last Friday.
Also, the inventory is being held by banks and a few merchants, which should result in occasional tightness.
Chinese production and exports could well hold the key to future price movements, with both output and shipments down on 1995 levels so far this year, traders said.
China National Non-ferrous Metals Import and Export Corp said in July that 1996 exports will fall to 20,000 to 35,000 tonnes, against 1995's 43,307 tonnes.
And on Monday, China's biggest tin producer said that production at the Gejiu mine in southern Yunnan had been cut by summer flooding, although business has not been affected.
